image_records.description: Technique: Sit or stand upright. Interlock hands and place the palms on the forehead. Pull the head back so that the nose points straight up to the ceiling. Muscles Stretched: Most-stretched muscle: Sternocleidomastoid. Lesser-stretched muscles: Longissimus capitis, semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, scalene. Commentary: You can do this stretch either while sitting or while standing. A greater stretch is applied when seated. Standing reduces the ability to stretch because reflexes come into play to prevent a loss of balance. During the stretch, make sure not to reduce the stretch by hunching up the shoulders. Also, try to point the chin as far back as possible.

The stretches in this chapter are excellent overall stretches; however, not all of these stretches may be completely suited to each person's needs. The muscles involved in the various neck movements appear in the following table. To stretch specific muscles, the stretch must involve one or more movements in the opposite direction of the desired muscle's movements. For example, if you want to stretch the left scalene, you could extend the head both backward and laterally to the right. When a muscle has a high level of stiffness, you should use fewer simultaneous opposite movements (you would stretch a very tight right scalene by initially doing just left lateral extension). As a muscle becomes loose, you can incorporate more simultaneous opposite movements.

Neck Extensor Stretch
Technique
Sit or stand upright.
Interlock hands on the back of the head near the crown.
Lightly pull the head straight down and try to touch the chin to the chest.

Muscles Stretched
Most-stretched muscle: Upper trapezius.
Lesser-stretched muscles: Longissimus capitis, semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, scalene.

Commentary
You can do this stretch either while sitting or while standing. A greater stretch is applied when seated. Standing reduces the ability to stretch because reflexes come into play to prevent a loss of balance. During the stretch, make sure not to reduce the stretch by hunching up the shoulders. Also, keep the neck as straight as possible (no curving). Try to touch the chin to the lowest possible point on the chest.

image_records.image_name: Neck Extensor and Rotation Stretch Technique
image_records.description: Variation: Neck Extensor and Rotation Stretch. Technique: Sit or stand upright. Place the right hand on the back of the head near the crown. Pull the head down toward the right and try to touch the chin as close as possible to the right shoulder. Muscles Stretched: Most-stretched muscles—Left upper trapezius, left sternocleidomastoid. Lesser-stretched muscles—Left longissimus capitis, left semispinalis capitis, left splenius capitis, left scalene. Anatomical labels shown: Sternocleidomastoid, Semispinalis capitis, Splenius capitis, Upper trapezius, Scalene.

Variation: Neck Flexor and Rotation Stretch. When the neck flexors become flexible, progress from stretching the right and left sides simultaneously to stretching the opposite sides individually. Technique: Stand or sit upright. Place right hand on the forehead. Pull the head back and toward the right so that the head points toward the shoulder. Keep the head straight; do not lay the head down to either side. Muscles Stretched: Most-stretched muscle—Left sternocleidomastoid. Lesser-stretched muscles—Left longissimus capitis, left semispinalis capitis, left splenius capitis.

image_records.image_name: Wrist Osteoarthritis Secondary to Malunited Fracture
image_records.description: This anteroposterior X-ray depicts a wrist with osteoarthritic changes secondary to scaphoid nonunion (SNAC), stage 2. Notable features visible in the image include the 'beaked' appearance of the radial styloid, cystic changes, a nonunion in the scaphoid, and 'kissing' osteophytes on the adjoining surfaces of the radius and scaphoid.

image_records.image_name: Wrist osteoarthritis secondary to malunited fracture
image_records.description: This radiograph depicts wrist osteoarthritis secondary to a malunited wrist fracture, identified as Figure 40.1 in the text. The image highlights dorsal angulation of the distal articular surface, reduced joint space, and significant osteopenia resulting from pain-induced lack of use.

image_records.image_name: Lateral radiograph of wrist with malunited fracture
image_records.description: This lateral X-ray (Figure 40.1) depicts wrist osteoarthritis secondary to a malunited wrist fracture. The image highlights dorsal angulation of the distal articular surface and reduced joint space, consistent with the caption's note on significant osteopenia.

image_records.image_name: Advanced wrist osteoarthritis secondary to SLAC stage 3
image_records.description: This radiograph depicts advanced wrist osteoarthritis secondary to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC), stage 3. As described in the associated caption (Figure 40.4), notable features include increased scapholunate space, sclerosis in the radioscaphoid and lunocapitate joints, proximal migration of the capitate, and a complete loss of normal wrist alignment.

image_records.image_name: Advanced SLAC Wrist Osteoarthritis Lateral Radiograph
image_records.description: Lateral view radiograph showing advanced wrist osteoarthritis secondary to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) stage 3. The image demonstrates increased scapholunate space, sclerosis in the radioscaphoid and lunocapitate joints, proximal migration of the capitate, and complete loss of normal wrist alignment.

Posteroanterior (PA) radiograph of the wrist showing the carpal bones, distal radius and ulna, and metacarpal bases. This view is used to evaluate carpal alignment, joint space narrowing, and degenerative changes associated with wrist osteoarthritis, scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC), or scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC).

image_records.image_name: Lateral Radiograph of SLAC Wrist Stage 2
image_records.description: This lateral X-ray (Figure 40.3 B) depicts wrist osteoarthritis secondary to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) at stage 2. The image reveals characteristic features including dorsal osteophytes and a dorsally angled lunate, indicating carpal instability and degenerative changes within the wrist joint.

The associated caption identifies it as the clinical appearance of an osteoarthritic wrist secondary to a scaphoid nonunion, noting that the diffuse radiodorsal swelling indicates some degree of synovitis.

image_records.image_name: Anteroposterior radiograph of wrist with osteoarthritis
image_records.description: Plain radiographs of the patient seen in Figure 40.3 after she underwent a proximal row carpectomy. A terminal radial styloidectomy has also been performed to reduce impingement of the trapezium on the tip of the radius. Note how well the capitate articulates with the lunate fossa of the distal radius.

image_records.image_name: Anteroposterior radiograph of wrist with osteoarthritis
image_records.description: This lateral X-ray view shows the postoperative appearance of a wrist following a scaphoid excision and four-bone fusion procedure. The image corresponds to Figure 40.9 B, illustrating the hardware used to maintain the fusion mass between the lunate, triquetrum, capitate, and hamate.

An intraoperative photograph (Figure 40.7) taken during a proximal row carpectomy procedure, showing exposed wrist anatomy with labeled structures including the pisiform, hamate, capitate, radio-lunate ligament, and radio-scapho capitate ligament. The image demonstrates healthy articular cartilage over the head of the capitate, which is a prerequisite for this motion-sparing surgical procedure used to treat SLAC and SNAC wrist arthritis.

This photograph depicts a patient's hands in a prayer position, illustrating postoperative function six months after a proximal row carpectomy. The associated caption notes that the patient has recovered nearly a 100-degree arc of motion and has no pain.

This image, labeled B, is part of Figure 40.8 illustrating postoperative function 6 months after a proximal row carpectomy. It shows the patient's hands demonstrating range of motion, consistent with the caption stating the patient has recovered nearly a 100-degree arc of motion and has no pain.

This X-ray image displays a wrist stabilized with multiple K-wires (pins) crossing the carpal bones. Based on the surrounding text and Figure 40.9 caption, this depicts a postoperative state following a scaphoid excision and four-bone fusion procedure, which involves fusing the lunate, triquetrum, capitate, and hamate.

image_records.image_name: Lateral radiograph of four-bone fusion with pins
image_records.description: This lateral radiograph depicts a wrist following a scaphoid excision and four-bone fusion procedure, stabilized with K-wires. It corresponds to Figure 40.9 B, which illustrates the postoperative appearance of the hardware used to maintain the fusion mass between the lunate, triquetrum, capitate, and hamate.

image_records.image_name: Postoperative radiograph of proximal row carpectomy
image_records.description: This lateral radiograph (labeled A) depicts a wrist following a proximal row carpectomy procedure. As indicated by the associated text and Figure 40.6 caption, the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum have been removed, allowing the capitate to articulate directly with the lunate fossa of the distal radius.

image_records.description: This lateral radiograph depicts a wrist joint with significant degenerative changes, identified in the surrounding text as the pre-operative state (Figure 40.3) of a patient who subsequently underwent a proximal row carpectomy. The image shows the distal radius, ulna, and carpal bones with irregularities and joint space narrowing consistent with

image_records.image_name: Total wrist arthrodesis with plate fixation
image_records.description: Anteroposterior radiograph showing a total wrist arthrodesis stabilized by a contoured metal plate and screws on the distal radius. The associated caption notes that the wrist is in mild ulnar deviation, which is the optimal position for hand function in such patients.

image_records.image_name: Lateral radiograph of total wrist arthrodesis
image_records.description: This image displays a lateral radiograph of a wrist that has undergone total wrist arthrodesis (fusion), stabilized with a contoured metal plate and screws. According to the associated caption (Figure 40.11), the wrist is positioned in mild dorsiflexion, which is considered the optimal position for hand function in such patients.

This posteroanterior radiograph (Figure 40.12) displays advanced degenerative disease of the wrist. The accompanying text uses this image to illustrate that motion-sparing procedures can eventually lead to further degeneration, characterized by significant joint space loss and sclerosis.

image_records.image_name: Proximal Articulation Components of the Tibia
image_records.description: This anatomical line drawing, identified as Figure 14.2 in the text, illustrates the proximal articulation components of the knee joint. It labels key structures including the distal femur with its condyles, the proximal tibia and fibula with their plateaus and intercondylar eminences, and the lateral and medial menisci.

image_records.image_name: Distal Articulation Components of the Femur
image_records.description: This anatomical diagram illustrates the distal articulation components of the femur, showing the lateral and medial femoral condyles, intercondylar groove, and cruciate ligaments (ACL and PCL). It also depicts the medial and lateral menisci situated between the femur and the tibia, with the fibula visible laterally. This image is identified as Figure 14.1 in the text on page 498, which discusses the osseous structures of the knee.

image_records.image_name: Inferior Posterior Surface of the Patella
image_records.description: This anatomical diagram illustrates the articular surface of the patella, labeling key features such as the superior border, superior and inferior medial facets, lateral facet, and the inferior pole. It corresponds to Figure 14.3 in the text, which describes the patella as a triangular sesamoid bone with concave surfaces for articulation with the femur.

image_records.image_name: Anterior View of the Tibiofemoral Joint
image_records.description: This anatomical illustration displays the anterior view of the knee joint, labeling key structures including the lateral and medial femoral condyles, menisci, tibia, fibula, and supracondylar ridges. It corresponds to Figure 14.4 in the text, which serves as a visual reference for the section on intraarticular structures.

image_records.image_name: Tibial Attachments of Medial and Lateral Menisci
image_records.description: This anatomical diagram, identified as Figure 14.5 in the surrounding text, illustrates a superior view of the knee joint's intraarticular structures. It labels the lateral and medial menisci, the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, and the insertion points of the posterior horns of the menisci.

image_records.image_name: Posterior View of Knee Cruciate Ligaments
image_records.description: This anatomical diagram displays a posterior view of the knee joint, labeling the femur, tibia, fibula, and the Anterior and Posterior Cruciate Ligaments. It corresponds to Figure 14.6 on page 501, which details the structural anatomy and function of these ligaments in stabilizing the knee.

image_records.image_name: Posterior View of Knee Joint Structures
image_records.description: This anatomical illustration displays the posterior aspect of the knee joint, labeling structures such as the femur, tibia, fibula, MCL, PCL, and Lateral Collateral Ligament. It corresponds to Figure 14.7 on page 502, which is referenced in the text describing the Lateral Collateral Ligament.

image_records.image_name: Anatomical Diagram of the Knee Joint
image_records.description: A labeled line drawing illustrating the anterior view of the knee joint, identifying the femur, tibia, fibula, medial and lateral menisci, and collateral ligaments. The text on page 502 references this as Figure 14.8, using it to illustrate the Medial Collateral Ligament Complex and its anatomical relationships.

This anatomical illustration depicts the posterior aspect of the knee joint, highlighting key structures such as the medial and lateral gastrocnemius origins, the lateral collateral ligament, the popliteal fibular ligament, the semimembranosus attachment, and the popliteus tendon. It corresponds to Figure 14.9 found on page 503, which is referenced in the text discussing posterolateral knee structures and posterior ligaments.

image_records.image_name: Active Physiological Knee Extension in Sitting
image_records.description: The image depicts a man sitting on an examination table with one leg extended straight forward, demonstrating active physiological knee extension. This corresponds to Figure 14.11, which illustrates a non-weight bearing active range-of-motion movement performed in a sitting position.

image_records.image_name: Active Physiological Knee Flexion in Sitting
image_records.description: This image shows a man sitting on an examination table with his right leg extended straight forward, demonstrating a specific physical therapy movement. It corresponds to Figure 14.11 on page 507, which is captioned 'Active Physiological Knee Flexion in Sitting' and is used to illustrate non-weight bearing active range-of-motion movements.

This image depicts a man performing a squat, which is identified in the accompanying text as 'The Functional Squat Test' (Figure 14.13). The text on page 507 explains that this test is used as an outcome measure for patients with knee osteoarthritis, involving squatting until pain limits the range or the heels come off the floor.

This image depicts a man performing the single step-down test (Figure 14.14), standing on a small platform with one foot while lowering his body. According to the text on page 507, this test is used to measure functional control of the knee during eccentric and concentric movements.

This image, identified as Figure 14.15, depicts a male subject performing a hop test by jumping on one leg with arms extended for balance. The accompanying text explains that this test is used to determine functional activity tolerance and predict dynamic knee stability, particularly for patients post-ACL reconstruction.

This image illustrates the technique for passive physiological knee flexion, identified as Figure 14.16 in the accompanying text. A clinician is shown holding a supine patient's leg to gently move the knee into flexion, assessing for range of motion and pain response.

Labeled as Figure 14.20, this image illustrates a manual therapy technique for knee extension with abduction. A clinician is shown grasping the patient's lateral ankle while the patient lies in a supine position to perform the movement.

Figure 14.21 Knee Extension with Adduction. Step Six: As the clinician extends the knee, using side bending of the trunk and a simultaneous force on these contact areas with the hands, the clinician then produces an extension-adduction movement of the knee (adduction movement of the tibia). Movement will occur up until pain is reproduced, then gently past this point as tolerated. Step Seven: As needed, the clinician can apply force (overpressure) to the end of range to assess for pain response.

image_records.image_name: Tibial Internal Rotation at 90 Degrees of Knee Flexion
image_records.description: This image depicts a clinician performing a manual therapy technique on a supine patient, specifically demonstrating tibial internal rotation. As identified in Figure 14.22 on page 511, the maneuver involves flexing the knee to approximately 90 degrees while the clinician cradles the tibia and grasps the foot to apply passive rotation.

Figure 14.23 Tibial External Rotation at 90 Degrees of Knee Extension. Step Four: The clinician applies a passive external rotation to the first point of pain. Repeated movements or sustained holds are applied to determine if the movements reduce pain. The activity is repeated toward end range.

image_records.image_name: Anterior-to-Posterior Mobilization of the Tibiofemoral Joint
image_records.description: The image depicts a clinician performing an anterior-to-posterior mobilization technique on a patient's knee. As identified by Figure 14.25 in the context, the clinician places thumbs on the tibial tubercle to gently move the tibia on the femur in a posterior direction.

image_records.image_name: Medial Glide of the Tibia on the Femur
image_records.description: This photograph, identified as Figure 14.28 in the accompanying text, depicts a clinician performing a medial shear mobilization on a patient's knee. It illustrates the technique described in the 'Medial and Lateral Shear of the Tibiofemoral Joint' section, where the clinician stabilizes the femur while applying a medially directed movement to the tibia.

image_records.image_name: Prone Compression Mobilization of the Tibiofemoral Joint
image_records.description: This image depicts a clinician performing a manual therapy technique on a patient lying in a prone position. It corresponds to Figure 14.64, illustrating the 'Compression Mobilization of the Tibial-Femoral Joint' where the clinician stabilizes the tibia and applies a compressive load.

image_records.image_name: Lateral Glide of Tibia on Femur
image_records.description: Figure 14.29 Lateral Glide of the Tibia on the Femur. Step Six: For lateral shear, the clinician uses one hand to grasp the lateral aspect of the distal femur, in the region of the condyles, while with the other hand the clinician grasps the lateral aspect of the proximal tibia. Step Seven: The clinician will stabilize the femur while applying a laterally directed movement of the tibia on the femur, stopping at the first point of pain.

image_records.image_name: Theoretical Movement of the Anterior Horn of the Meniscus
image_records.description: This line drawing diagram illustrates the anatomy of the knee joint, specifically labeling the femur, tibia, fibula, and anterior horn of the meniscus. It depicts a mobilization setup with a block placed under the posterior femur, demonstrating the theoretical movement where posterior glide of the tibia on the femur results in anterior movement of the meniscus.

image_records.image_name: Theoretical Movement of the Posterior Horn of the Meniscus
image_records.description: This diagram illustrates the theoretical movement of the posterior horn of the meniscus within the knee joint, showing the femur, tibia, and fibula. It corresponds to Figure 14.27, which demonstrates how anterior movement of the tibia on the femur in a flexed position forces posterior migration of the meniscus.

Figure 14.30 Medial and Anterior Rotation of the Tibia on the Femur. Step One: The patient assumes a hooklying position. The clinician stabilizes the foot by sitting on the dorsum. Step Two: The clinician grabs the lateral half of the tibia with one hand and stabilizes the femur with the other. The clinician then applies a medially directed and anterior rotation to the lateral half of the tibia.

This image depicts a manual therapy technique where a clinician places their fingers against the medial border of a patient's patella to perform a lateral glide. It corresponds to Figure 14.36 on page 518, which is part of the section on 'Medial and Lateral Movements of the Patellofemoral Joint'.

This image depicts a manual therapy technique known as the medial glide of the patella, corresponding to Figure 14.37. It shows a clinician's hands positioned on either side of the patient's knee to produce a medially directed movement of the patella.

This image depicts a clinician performing a medial tilt maneuver on a patient's patella, corresponding to Figure 14.38 in the provided text. The hands are positioned on the knee to push the medial half of the patella in an anterior-to-posterior direction, illustrating a technique from the 'Medial and Lateral Tilt Movements of the Patellofemoral Joint' section.

Figure 14.39 Lateral Tilt of the Patella. Step Six: To create a lateral tilt, the clinician can follow the above steps, but will produce lateral tilting movement by producing movement in an anterior-to-posterior direction on the lateral half of the patella. The clinician should also be sure to block the medial border of the patella to prevent a medial movement of the patella during the lateral tilting movement.

This image depicts a clinician performing a manual therapy technique on a patient's knee, specifically grasping the patella with both hands. Based on the accompanying text in Chapter 14, this corresponds to Figure 14.40, illustrating the 'Medial Rotation of the Patella' where the clinician rotates the apex of the patella medially while the patient is in a supine position.

Figure 14.40 Medial Rotation of the Patella. Step Three: To produce a medially directed rotation, the clinician will rotate the apex of the patella medially, stopping at the first point of pain. The clinician may find it helpful when producing these movements to take up tissue slack around the knee. This can be accomplished by placing the hands on the patella as described in Step Two (the following describes medially directed movement) but place the cephalic hand medially (about the 2 o'clock position) and the caudal hand just opposite the cephalic hand (about the 8 o'clock position). Now firmly grasping the soft tissues move your hands back to the original position. This technique should allow the clinician to feel more localized movement of the patella versus the surrounding soft tissues. Step Four: The clinician will assess for quality of motion and assess for reproduction of concordant signs while moving the patella beyond the first point of pain, progressing toward end range as the patient's complaint of pain allows. Step Five: Repeated movements are then performed to the point of range/movement that pain allows, to assess the response of the repeated movements on the patient's pain (or like symptoms).
Figure 14.65 Supine Compression Mobilization of the Tibiofemoral Joint. Step Four: The procedure can also be performed using similar hand-holds with the patient in a supine position.

The image depicts a person sitting on a treatment table holding their knee, illustrating the 'Posterior Anterior Scoop Mobilization' technique labeled as Figure 14.66. The accompanying text explains that this mobilization targets the posterior horn of the meniscus and involves a curvilinear posterior-to-anterior pull near end-range flexion.

image_records.image_name: Compression Mobilization of the Tibiofemoral Joint
image_records.description: The image depicts a clinician performing a manual therapy technique on a patient's knee while the patient is in a prone position. Based on the text in the following page (Figure 14.65), this image illustrates the prone variation of the 'Compression Mobilization of the Tibiofemoral Joint,' where the clinician applies a load to the tibia.

Figure 14.43 Anterior to Posterior Glide of the Tibial Fibular Joint. Step One: The patient assumes the sidelying position with the area examined facing upward. The clinician should aim to position the lower extremity in a relatively neutral position (i.e., pillow between knees, etc.). Step Two: The clinician stands in front of the patient and palpates for the posterior margin of the head of the fibula. Step Three: The clinician then places the pads of his or her thumbs against the anterior margin of the head of the fibula. Step Four: Using the thumbs, produce a posterior-to-anterior directed movement, stopping at the first point of pain. Step Five: The clinician will assess for quality of motion and assess for reproduction of concordant signs while moving the fibula beyond the first point of pain, progressing toward end range as the patient's complaint of pain allows. Step Six: Repeated movements are then performed to the point of range/movement that pain allows, to assess the response of the repeated movements on the patient's pain (or like symptoms). Step Seven: The previously described movements should then be performed with compression. This is achieved by leaving one thumb on the anterior margin of the fibula and taking the interthenar groove of the other hand and placing it on top of the thumb. Compression is achieved by pushing downward toward the table while simultaneously producing the anterior-to-posterior movement. Steps Five and Six are then followed while using compression.

This image, labeled as Figure 14.44, depicts a clinician performing a manual therapy technique on a patient's lower leg while the patient is in a sidelying position. It illustrates the 'Cephalic Glide of the Fibula' as part of the assessment for the Tibial-Fibular Joint, where the clinician grasps the rear-foot to produce movement.

This image depicts a clinician performing McMurray's test, a clinical special test for meniscal tears. It corresponds to Figure 14.48 found on page 525, showing the manipulation of the patient's knee.

This image depicts a clinician performing Apley's Compression Test, which is labeled as Figure 14.49 on page 526. The patient is lying in a prone position with the knee flexed, while the clinician grasps the foot to apply a compressive force through the tibia to test for meniscal injuries.

This image depicts the Apley's Distraction Test, identified as Figure 14.50 in the accompanying text. It shows a clinician applying a distraction force and twisting motion to a patient's knee while the patient lies prone, a procedure used to differentiate between meniscal and capsuloligamentous injuries.

This image illustrates the Pivot Shift Test, a clinical assessment used to detect anterior cruciate ligament instability. It depicts a clinician holding a patient's leg at the ankle and knee while the patient lies supine, preparing to guide the knee into extension to observe for subluxation and reduction.

This image depicts a clinician performing the Posterior Drawer Test on a patient's knee. As identified in the text on page 530 (Figure 14.54), this clinical special test is designed to measure posterior displacement of the tibia on a fixed femur to detect Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) instability.

This image illustrates the Posterior Sag Sign, a clinical test used to detect posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) instability. It depicts a clinician holding a patient's foot while the patient lies supine with the hip and knee flexed, allowing for visual assessment of posterior tibial translation.

This image depicts a clinician performing the Quadriceps Active Test on a patient lying in a supine position. Identified as Figure 14.56 in the accompanying text, the procedure involves the patient flexing their hip to 45 degrees and knee to 90 degrees while the clinician assesses for anterior tibial translation.

image_records.image_name: The Dial Test Performed in Prone at 90 Degrees
image_records.description: This image depicts a clinician performing the Dial Test on a patient lying prone with knees flexed. According to the accompanying text, this test is designed to determine isolated posterolateral corner instability by comparing external rotation of the knees.

The image depicts a clinician performing the Vastus Medialis Coordination Test on a patient lying in a supine position. The clinician supports the patient's leg, which is slightly flexed, while the patient is instructed to extend the knee slowly to assess coordination.

This image illustrates the Patellar Apprehension Test, labeled as Figure 14.61, where a clinician applies a lateral glide to the patient's knee cap while the patient lies in a supine position to check for pain or apprehension.

This image depicts a clinician performing Clarke's Test on a patient lying in a supine position. The clinician applies an inferior force and slight compression to the patella while the patient is instructed to contract their quadriceps to assess for patellofemoral grinding pain.

This image, identified as Figure 14.63, depicts a patient performing the Eccentric Step Test by standing on a step with arms extended for balance. The associated text explains that the test involves an eccentric load to the knee during a controlled step down to reproduce pain.

image_records.image_name: Tibial Shear at 90 Degrees of Flexion
image_records.description: This image shows a clinician performing a manual therapy technique on a patient's knee, specifically a tibial shear mobilization. Identified as Figure 14.68 in the text, the procedure is described as targeting the knee capsule when performed at greater degrees of flexion.

image_records.image_name: Rotation Mobilization at 90 Degrees of Flexion
image_records.description: This image displays a close-up view of a clinician's hands clasped around a patient's lower leg to perform a rotational mobilization technique. It corresponds to Figure 14.69, which illustrates 'Rotation Mobilization at 90 Degrees of Flexion' within the context of tibial rotation at multiple ranges.

This image, identified as Figure 14.70 on page 539, depicts a clinician performing an isometric hold-relax hamstring stretch on a supine patient. The accompanying text describes the technique where the patient's leg is prepositioned in a 90/90 posture and the clinician braces the patient's heel while the patient performs an isometric contraction.

image_records.image_name: Tibiofemoral Distraction Manipulation of the Knee
image_records.description: This image depicts a clinician performing a tibiofemoral distraction manipulation on a patient lying in a prone position. The associated text describes the technique as a rapid distraction of the tibia from the femur, which is used to treat knee conditions.
